\section{System Model}
\label{sec:system}

We consider a LEO satellite-enabled grant-free random access system,
where AFDM is adopted to mitigate the doubly dispersive effect inherent
in terrestrial-satellite links (TSLs) \cite{ding2026,bemani2022}.
The system comprises $K$ single-antenna terrestrial devices that
communicate with a LEO satellite equipped with a uniform planar array
(UPA) consisting of $M=M_yM_z$ antennas. During each transmission
block, active devices share the same time-frequency resources to
transmit their pilots to the satellite. Additionally, to minimize
energy consumption, we assume that these terrestrial devices operate
without GNSS capabilities and do not pre-compensate for delay and
Doppler shifts. After compensating for the common propagation delay
$\tau_c$, the satellite receiver handles the differential delay and
Doppler shift observed in the uplink transmission \cite{shen2025}.

\subsection{Terrestrial-Satellite Link Model}

The TSLs will experience fast variations due to the high mobility of
the LEO satellite. Hence, this time variation and multipath propagation
require a doubly dispersive channel model for accurate TSLs
characterization \cite{shen2025}. Take the ground device as the
stationary reference point. The resulting Doppler term $\nu_k$ is
assumed to be common to all propagation paths within the same TSL
\cite{huang2026}. As a result of the long distance between the satellite
and device $k$, the angles-of-arrival for different paths tend to be
identical \cite{li2023}. Let $\mathbf a_k$ denote the array response
vector of device $k$. Then, the time-varying channel impulse response
from the $k$th device to the satellite can be represented as
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf h_k(t,\tau)
 =\mathbf a_k\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_k}g_{k\ell}
 e^{j2\pi\nu_k t}\delta(\tau-\tau_{k\ell}),
 \label{eq:physical-channel}
\end{equation}
where $L_k$ is the number of propagation paths, $g_{k\ell}$ denotes
the complex channel coefficient associated with the $\ell$th path,
and $\delta(\cdot)$ represents the Dirac delta function.
$\tau_{k\ell}=\widetilde\tau_{k\ell}-\tau_c$ represents the differential
delay for the $\ell$th path from the $k$th device to the satellite,
where $\widetilde\tau_{k\ell}$ and $\tau_c$ are denoted as propagation
delay and common delay, respectively. The common delay corresponds
to the propagation time between the satellite and the closest point
on earth within the beam coverage \cite{shen2025}.
Let $t$ denote the time measured from the start of the transmission
block. The array response vector $\mathbf a_k$ can be represented as
\begin{equation}
 [\mathbf a_k]_{n_z+M_zn_y}
 =e^{j2\pi(d_yn_y\mu_{y,k}+d_zn_z\mu_{z,k})/\lambda},
 \label{eq:upa}
\end{equation}
where $\mu_{y,k}$ and $\mu_{z,k}$ are the directional cosines, $d_y$
and $d_z$ are the antenna spacings, $\lambda$ is the wavelength,
$0\leq n_y<M_y$, and $0\leq n_z<M_z$. Assume that the path gains,
differential delays, Doppler shifts, and angles-of-arrival remain
approximately constant within a transmission block.
The time variation in \eqref{eq:physical-channel} is therefore
determined by $e^{j2\pi\nu_k t}$.

\subsection{Multi-Frame AFDM Transmission}

The multi-frame AFDM transmission scheme is proposed to handle the
large differential delay and Doppler shift.
Assume that a total of $Q$ AFDM frames are allocated for pilot
transmission. Specifically, in the $q$th AFDM frame,
$q=0,\ldots,Q-1$, the $k$th device is assigned a pilot vector
$\mathbf p_{qk}\in\mathbb C^N$, with $[\mathbf p_{qk}]_n=P_{qkn}$,
where $N$ is the number of AFDM chirp subcarriers and $\Delta f$ is
the subcarrier spacing. The $N$ pilot symbols have energy
$\|\mathbf p_{qk}\|^2=E_p$. Different pilot vectors, known at the
satellite receiver, are used across frames.
The time-domain transmitted signal is generated through the inverse
discrete affine Fourier transform (IDAFT) applied to $\mathbf p_{qk}$,
mathematically formulated as
$\mathbf s_{qk}=\mathbf F_{\rm A}^{\mathsf H}\mathbf p_{qk}$
\cite{ding2026}, where $\mathbf F_{\rm A}$ denotes the discrete
affine Fourier transform (DAFT) matrix, given by
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 [\mathbf F_{\rm A}]_{rt}
 =\frac{1}{\sqrt N}e^{-j2\pi(c_2r^2+rt/N+c_1t^2)},\\
 r,t=0,\ldots,N-1.
 \end{gathered}
 \label{eq:daft}
\end{equation}
Here, $c_1$ and $c_2$ are AFDM modulation parameters, and
$T_s=1/(N\Delta f)$ gives the sampling interval.

Assume that the chirp-periodic prefix (CPP) duration satisfies
$N_{\rm CPP}T_s\geq\max_{k,\ell}\tau_{k\ell}$.
With the chirp periodicity, the prefix is \cite{bemani2022}
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 s_{qk}[t]=e^{j2\pi c_1(t^2-\langle t\rangle_N^2)}
 s_{qk}[\langle t\rangle_N],\\
 -N_{\rm CPP}\leq t<0,
 \end{gathered}
 \label{eq:cpp}
\end{equation}
where $\langle x\rangle_N=x-N\lfloor x/N\rfloor$ and
$2Nc_1\in\mathbb N_+$. The prefix prevents inter-frame interference
even when the differential delay exceeds $NT_s$.
$T_{\rm frame}=(N+N_{\rm CPP})T_s$ is the time duration of an AFDM
frame with CPP.

After removing the CPP and applying the DAFT, let
$H_k^{(q)}\in\mathbb C^{M\times N\times N}$ denote the effective
channel of device $k$ in frame $q$, with $H_k=H_k^{(0)}$.
To better capture the LEO channel dynamics, we incorporate
fractional delay and fractional Doppler effects, and the resulting
expression for the elements of $H_k$ is given as follows
\cite{huang2026}:
\begin{equation}
 H_{kmrn}
 =[\mathbf a_k]_m\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_k}g_{k\ell}
 [\mathbf G(\tau_{k\ell}/T_s,\nu_k;N_{\rm CPP})]_{rn}.
 \label{eq:channel}
\end{equation}
Here, $H_{kmrn}$ is the channel coefficient from transmitted
DAFT-domain symbol $n$ to received DAFT-domain symbol $r$ at
antenna $m$. $\mathbf G(d,\nu;N_{\rm CPP})$ denotes the effective
channel matrix of a path with gain $1$, normalized delay $d$, and
Doppler shift $\nu$ in frame $0$.
For the $N$ samples after CPP removal, starting at sample $g$,
this matrix is given by
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathbf G(d,\nu;g)=\mathbf F_{\rm A}\mathbf D_{\nu,g}\mathbf B_d,\\
 \mathbf D_{\nu,g}=\diag\{e^{j2\pi\nu T_s(g+t)}\}_{t=0}^{N-1},\\
 [\mathbf B_d]_{tn}=\varphi_n(t-d).
 \end{gathered}
 \label{eq:path-operator-system}
\end{equation}
Here, $\varphi_n$ is the transmitted waveform when the $n$th
DAFT-domain symbol equals $1$ and all other input symbols are zero,
with the CPP defined in \eqref{eq:cpp}. Its expression and the
derivation of \eqref{eq:path-operator-system} for fractional delays,
including delays exceeding $NT_s$, are given in
Appendix~\ref{app:afdm-model}. For frame $0$, $g=N_{\rm CPP}$.
In practical propagation environments, fractional Doppler shifts
and fractional time delays can introduce significant power leakage
in the effective channel matrix, thereby weakening its sparsity
\cite{huang2026}. To address this issue, we retain the full
$N\times N$ channel matrix at each antenna.

Furthermore, the phase rotation $e^{j2\pi\nu_kqT_{\rm frame}}$
caused by the Doppler shift $\nu_k$ accumulates across multiple
frames \cite{shen2025}. Since $\nu_k$ is common to all paths of
device $k$, \eqref{eq:physical-channel} yields
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 H_k^{(q)}=e^{jq\beta_k}H_k,\\
 \beta_k=\operatorname{wrap}(2\pi\nu_kT_{\rm frame}),
 \end{gathered}
 \label{eq:twc-frame-channel}
\end{equation}
where $\operatorname{wrap}(\cdot)$ maps an angle to $[-\pi,\pi)$.
After separating the inter-frame phase rotation in
\eqref{eq:twc-frame-channel}, $H_k$ remains approximately constant
over $Q$ consecutive frames.
This characteristic allows the proposed scheme to gather more
observations, thereby facilitating channel estimation without
increasing the number of channel coefficients to be estimated.

We use an indicator function $\alpha_k\in\{0,1\}$ to model the
device activity, where $\alpha_k=1$ if the $k$th device is active,
and $\alpha_k=0$ otherwise. Let $\rho$ represent the probability
of a device being active, i.e., $\Pr(\alpha_k=1)=\rho$.
Each device maintains its activity state throughout a transmission
block. Let $X_k=\alpha_kH_k$.
According to the superposition principle, the $q$th received frame
in the DAFT domain is given by
\begin{equation}
 Y_{qmr}=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}A_{qkn}X_{kmrn}+W_{qmr},
 \label{eq:observation-tensor}
\end{equation}
where $W_{qmr}$ are i.i.d.\ drawn from $\CN(0,\sigma^2)$, and
\begin{equation}
 A_{qkn}=P_{qkn}e^{jq\beta_k}
 \label{eq:effective-pilot}
\end{equation}
is the pilot symbol multiplied by the phase rotation in
\eqref{eq:twc-frame-channel}.
Next, we collect the $Q$ received frames into a single matrix as
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf Y=\mathbf A\mathbf X+\mathbf W,
 \label{eq:mmv}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf Y,\mathbf W\in\mathbb C^{Q\times MN}$,
$\mathbf A\in\mathbb C^{Q\times KN}$ has entries
$[\mathbf A]_{q,(k-1)N+n}=A_{qkn}$, and
$\mathbf X\in\mathbb C^{KN\times MN}$ is defined together with
$\mathbf Y$ by
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 [\mathbf Y]_{q,mN+r}&=Y_{qmr},\\
 [\mathbf X]_{(k-1)N+n,mN+r}&=X_{kmrn}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:mmv-indexing}
\end{equation}
The column index is $mN+r$, and each device occupies $N$ rows
indexed by its transmitted symbol $n$.
Let $\mathbf P\in\mathbb C^{Q\times KN}$ denote the pilot matrix,
with entries $[\mathbf P]_{q,(k-1)N+n}=P_{qkn}$.
For simplicity, we impose the condition that $\mathbf P$ is partial
orthogonal, specifically requiring that
$\mathbf P\mathbf P^{\mathsf H}=KE_p\I_Q$.
The design of partial orthogonal $\mathbf P$ is deferred to
Section~\ref{sec:simulation-settings}.

Due to the sporadic access of the devices, matrix $\mathbf X$
exhibits a block-sparsity structure. Specifically, if the $k$th
device is inactive, we have $X_k=\alpha_kH_k=\mathbf 0$
\cite{cai2026}.
The channel coefficients within each active block are statistically
dependent through the common path parameters and array response
in \eqref{eq:channel}.

\subsection{Problem Formulation}

In this paper, we aim to simultaneously detect the active devices
and estimate the corresponding channels based on the observation
$\mathbf Y$ under a Bayesian inference framework \cite{cai2026}.
We consider $Q<KN$ in \eqref{eq:mmv}.

In this subsection, we assume that the estimates
$\widehat{\mathbf A}$ and $\widehat\sigma^2$ are known, which are
obtained from $\mathbf Y$ as described in Section~\ref{sec:frontend}.
Let $q_{\rm tr}$ denote the prior distribution of $H_k$ represented
by the channel samples used for training.
For inference, we assume independence across devices and between
each device's activity and channel. The activities follow Bernoulli
priors, while $q_{\rm tr}(H_k)$ retains the dependence among the
coefficients within $H_k$.

Exact Bayesian estimators, e.g., the MMSE estimator, are generally
intractable due to the high-dimensional integrals in the
marginalization of the joint posterior distribution.
Alternatively, message-passing algorithms provide a low-complexity
iterative approach for approximately calculating the MMSE estimator
\cite{cai2026}. In message passing, we factorize the joint posterior
distribution according to Bayes' theorem and the conditional
independence relationships among the variables, expressed as
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 &q(\mathbf X,\{H_k\},\bm\alpha\mid\mathbf Y)\\
 &\quad\propto p(\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf X)\\
 &\qquad\times\prod_{k=1}^{K}
 p(X_k\mid H_k,\alpha_k)q_{\rm tr}(H_k)p(\alpha_k),
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:working-posterior}
\end{equation}
where $p(\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf X)$ is the Gaussian likelihood from
\eqref{eq:mmv}, $p(X_k\mid H_k,\alpha_k)$ imposes
$X_k=\alpha_kH_k$, and
$p(\alpha_k)=\rho^{\alpha_k}(1-\rho)^{1-\alpha_k}$.
The MMSE channel estimate and posterior probability of activity
can be calculated as
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 X_k^{\rm MMSE}&=\E_q[X_k\mid\mathbf Y],\\
 p_k^{\rm Bayes}&=q(\alpha_k=1\mid\mathbf Y).
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:targets}
\end{equation}

The main difficulty in implementing message passing on the factor
graph lies in the message calculation associated with the factor
node $q_{\rm tr}(H_k)$ \cite{cai2026}.
Generally speaking, even if the ground-truth channel distribution
becomes analytically available, calculating the messages for the
factor node $q_{\rm tr}(H_k)$ remains highly challenging due to the
complicated and high-dimensional integrals. To summarize, the
message-passing framework faces a dilemma: the adopted channel
prior is either too imprecise to ensure good performance, or too
complex to facilitate efficient message calculation.
This paper seeks to address the aforementioned challenges by
plugging in deep generative priors for efficient message calculation.
